newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela opposes Tutu over amnesty extension.
newsitem.headline: Mandela opposes Tutu over amnesty extension.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Friday he was opposed to extending the cut-off date for crimes eligible for political amnesty to include a last-ditch pre-election bombing campaign in 1994.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu, head of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, said he spent an hour with Mandela on Thursday trying to persuade him to extend the commission's mandate and to ensure that former guerrillas of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) participate.
Mandela told reporters that Tutu had asked him to extend the cut-off date for amnesty by five months to May 10, 1994, when he was installed as South Africa's first black president.
"We are facing the serious situation of a high level of crime and extending the cut-off date would send a wrong signal.

"I am determined personally -- my views are set on this question -- but because of my respect for Archbishop Tutu...I will ask that he should appear before the cabinet to put his views directly," Mandela said.
The cabinet has already rejected a similar request.

The existing cut-off date marks the multiparty agreement on December 6, 1993, on terms for a transition to democracy and excludes right-wingers who killed 21 people in bomb attacks designed to derail the April 26 election that ended white rule.
It also rules out black supremacist Pan Africanist Congress members blamed for attacks including the killing of four New Year revellers in a Cape Town pub.
Mandela said the existing date included all those who backed the decision to move to democracy and said the significance of his inauguration did not justify a change.
Tutu lambasted provincial premier Mathews Phosa, head of the ANC's legal department, for saying that former ANC guerrillas did not need amnesty for "acts of war" against white rule.
Phosa said ANC guerrillas responsible for bombings, shootings and other killings in the war against white rule were engaged in a legitimate war.
The ANC has always refused to equate its struggle with the white government's attempt to defend minority rule, but Mandela said Phosa's views were his own and not the ANC's.
Tutu said former white generals and ministers responsible for human rights abuses could make the same excuse.
"If people grant themselves amnesty, what is the point of the commission...Why don't they go ahead and just give themselves a general amnesty," he said.
Tutu's 173 million rand ($38 million) commission has 30 months to investigate the human rights record of the war over apartheid, to pardon perpetrators and to compensate victims.

After a slow start, former agents of the apartheid regime have started to talk about their campaign against the ANC, implicating former government ministers and presidents in decisions to blow up buildings and target individual activists.
On Thursday, the commission subpoenaed a former police general for the first time to answer allegations made by victims of apartheid and on Friday another was called in.
The ANC has admitted to only a handful of offences and no leading member of the party has yet applied for amnesty.

"I am calling on the ANC to make a clear statement that its members and leaders will apply for amnesty for any act in respect of which they may be liable for prosecution or actions for civil damages," Tutu said.
